questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: Good creative writing and anthropology programs and great natural surroundings.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think it was quite easy. There were introduction activities and helpful front desk services all around.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was attached to a "buddy," who helped my get settled in my classes. Other exchange students helped out as well.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I was one of the only student who were granted on campus accommodation for a single term exchange. I was happy with the opportunity as it was cheaper than finding a place on my own and it was nice to stay with other students. The accommodation is nothing spectacular and life on campus gets quite grey and boring in the winter, but for me it was the right fit.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: There was an option to get a meal plan through UBC, but there was also a well functioning kitchen, where I cooked all my meals.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: It's convenient and somewhat cheaper than many other options, but it gets grey and sad during winter time. In the beginning it's hard to find time to get off campus and explore the city. Mostly everything you need is available on campus though, just a little expensive (especially groceries).

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There is a fine website where you browse courses and it clearly states which are full or restricted. I found it very straight forward.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: To register for courses you list as many courses as you wish and they will assign you to five or so. The first two weeks of term you then have the opportunity to move around a bit. I ended up doing three courses instead of five as this was the demand from my home university.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Not a lot of help during this process, but I didn't look for it either.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got into all the classes I wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Try out as many courses as possible, but do as few at a time as you can - the workload is quite heavy at UBC.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I did mainly 300-level anthropology courses (my major) and one 200-level creative writing course. I liked them all, and found the level not too challenging. I could have taken 400-level instead no problem. The lower level courses will "baby" you more and give you many assignments to keep track of your work. The upper level courses have more freedom, but are obviously more complex as well.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: Less participatory lectures, no seminars in my courses. I enjoyed the teaching style of all my profs, but they definitely didn't demand as much in-class participation or discussion as courses at UCPH. Also, they require more assignments during the term, which keeps you on top of things.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: ANTH341 -Anthropology of Museums, Heritage and Memory, ANTH378- Anthropology of Media, CRWR205 - Introduction to Writing Creative Non-Fiction.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed all my courses, but mainly recommend CRWR205. UCPH doesn't offer courses in CRWR and it's a great way to develop your English language skills while you are here. The prof is amazing and engaging. I never missed a class. ANTH341 is interesting while being in Canada as it gives you some insight to Canadian history and indigenous politics. The prof is a little shy though, but I enjoyed her lectures none the less. ANTH378 was a classic and really good ANTH course, non-anth students could take it as well.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Food! So expensive to go grocery shopping. Also, if you want to go on many trips it will be expensive. Whistler/skiing in general is super pricy.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing was slightly more than I anticipated for on campus housing, but similar or better than many other places in the city. Food was so, so expensive. Also, no cheap coffee on campus.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: So many clubs and societies available. Joined the surf-club and yoga-club, but I'm sad I didn't join the Varsity Outdoor Club (VOC) - old society at UBC that arranges all sorts of hiking, climbing, skiing etc. trips.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go on surf trips to Tofino and ski trips to Whistler. Join the VOC! The yoga club has lots of classes on campus and is quite cheap. Also take advantage of the aquatic center with a morning swim every once in a while.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Go on as
many.trips.as
.possible. Don't hold back. Go hiking, skiing, surfing. Don't expect to much of Vancouver (it's called Raincouver and the No-Fun City). Nightlife is non-existent and everything is expensive. Take the trips.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, similar to home. Canadians are adventurous and kind!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Join VOC, Surf Club and other societies. And talk to people in your courses! Not just the exchange students. People are really nice, so don't be too shy.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Not really anything. Maybe the politeness - I felt quite rude in comparison.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Kindness, adventure, language. People really love and take advantage of the mountains.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Don't expect too much from the city, go on as many trips as possible and make the first move to get friends!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be prepared for food to be expensive. Be organized and take trips to cheaper super markets. Make the most of your stay, it goes by pretty fast.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Ski season! And all of the sweet international students I got to meet.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It was expensive and I didn't enjoy the city. It got cold, grey and wet in the winter and before ski season starts it can be quite depressing. Workload on courses was heavier than what I'm used to at UCPH, although it wasn't more difficult.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
